newsitem.title: ITALY: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI LEADS ITALY TO SLALOM GOLD.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-COMPAGNONI LEADS ITALY TO SLALOM GOLD.

text.p: Double Olympic gold medallist Deborah Compagnoni led home an Italian one-two at the Alpine skiing world championships on Wednesday to crown herself Italy's first women's slalom world champion.
The world and Olympic giant slalom champion clocked one minute 43.88 seconds down the floodlit Kandahar piste.
On a memorable night for the host nation, Lara Magoni stormed through from seventh place after the first leg to take the silver medal a huge 1.27 seconds behind.

Karin Roten, who had been fastest in the first leg of the night-time slalom just 0.05 ahead of Compagnoni, failed to deliver Switzerland's first world championship gold medal since 1993 and had to settle for the bronze.
"This is the greatest day of my life," declared the 26-year-old champion, who gained her first World Cup slalom victory in December and her first win in Italy last month.
"To win this gold medal in Italy and in front of my home crowd is just incredible.
"I just went for it, I was unleashed. I didn't ski so well but I was really fast."

Compagnoni, whose four World Cup wins this season have also sparked what has been popularly dubbed "Debbymania" in Italy, now joins her compatriot Alberto Tomba as a double world champion. Tomba has a career five world and Olympic golds to her four.
She was also the second champion from Sierra Nevada last year to strike gold again. Men's super-giant slalom champion Atle Skaardal of Norway retained his title on Monday.
Magoni, whose career has been hit by injury just like Compagnoni's, had signalled her comeback with a second place in a slalom in Laax this month after a third in Maribor.
She dedicated her silver to all the world's sick.
"It is wonderful to be on the podium with Deborah because we have both had so many injuries," she said.
"I'm 28 years old but I feel like 20."
While the home crowd exploded with delight, Roten felt she had scored at least a moral victory with bronze.
The Swiss, a giant slalom silver medallist behind Compagnoni at last year's championships, said that having to follow the Italians down the piste had been almost impossible.
"I went out and all the people, all the volunteers at the start, were shouting 'You won't make it'," she said.
"In these conditions I am proud of myself."
The top six after the first leg had been just 0.18 seconds behind Roten but the piste soon sorted them out.
Defending champion Pernilla Wiberg of Sweden, ninth after the first leg, attacked a touch too aggressively in the second and went crashing out after missing a gate.
The Swede, who has five gold medals in her career, also made an error at the top of the piste on the first leg.
"I felt lazy in the first run. It didn't feel like a world championship race. I was just trying too hard to go for it and I hooked a tip. But that's slalom."
She was the first of a string of fallers.

Sabine Egger of Austria fell almost immediately and Austrian-born Claudia Riegler, who races for New Zealand and has won three World Cup slaloms this season, followed her after hooking the fourth gate and sliding down the piste.
"I took a lot of risks," said Riegler, who has won three World Cup slaloms this season but who had complained that the freezing cold night air had made breathing difficult.
"I was not so nervous for the second leg. I had a chance and went for it. Straddling a gate is part of the game."
Marlies Oester, another Swiss medal hope after finishing the first leg fourth, also crashed out.

A major surprise was Briton Emma Carrick-Anderson who came from the 41st starting place to complete the first leg 14th fastest, 1.58 seconds behind Roten, and moved up on the second run to finish 11th.
